input:
In this example, we consider a countercurrent heat exchanger in which a process stream is cooled from 120 °C to 85 °C by means of cooling water, which enters the exchanger at 30 °C and leaves at 55 °C. In order to characterise the temperature driving force within the exchanger, it is necessary to evaluate the temperature differences at the two ends of the unit. At the end where the hot stream enters, the temperature difference is 120 − 55 = 65 K, whilst at the end where the hot stream leaves, the difference is 85 − 30 = 55 K. The appropriate mean temperature difference for this situation is the log-mean temperature difference, $\Delta T_{lm}$, which is related to the two terminal differences, $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$, by the following well-known expression:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

Substituting $\Delta T_1$ = 65 K and $\Delta T_2$ = 55 K into this expression, the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is found to be 59.9 K. It is important to note that this log-mean value is based on the assumptions of a constant overall heat transfer coefficient and no phase change taking place in either of the streams; where these assumptions do not hold, the calculated value should be treated with appropriate caution.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 120 °C to 85 °C. Water enters at 30 °C and leaves at 55 °C. At the end where the hot stream enters, the temperature difference is 120 − 55 = 65 K; at the end where the hot stream leaves, the difference is 85 − 30 = 55 K. The log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ follows from the two terminal differences $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

With $\Delta T_1$ = 65 K and $\Delta T_2$ = 55 K, $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 59.9 K. The value lies between the two terminal differences and just below their arithmetic mean, as a log mean must when the two terminal differences are close to each other. The log mean is the mean difference that, used with a constant overall coefficient, gives the duty the exchanger actually transfers over its area. The log-mean value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream; a coefficient that varies with temperature, or a stream that condenses or boils along the exchanger, takes the calculation outside the stated basis. Countercurrent flow is what keeps the difference at the cold end positive here: the water leaves against the entering hot stream, so the two terminal differences are the pair the equation takes.
